Welcome back. Everything on this page runs real R in your browser — same setup as Coding Activity 2. You already pulled a column and computed a mean; today you will **summarize** a variable with standard tools for **center** (typical value) and **spread** (how much values vary).

The first time you click **Run Code**, your browser downloads R once (a few seconds). After that it is quick.

::: {.callout-note}
## Center and spread in one sentence

- **Center** — where most values sit (`mean()`, `median()`).
- **Spread** — how far values scatter from that center (`sd()`, `IQR()`).

Always say **units** when you report a number (grams for body mass here).
:::

## 1. Load body mass

Run this to load Palmer Penguins and store body mass in grams. Two penguins have missing weights (`NA`); we skip those in every summary below.

```{webr}
#| envir: global
library(palmerpenguins)
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
head(body_mass)
```

## 2. Center: mean and median

Compute the **mean** and **median** of `body_mass`, each with `na.rm = TRUE`. Run both lines. (If you skipped the cell above, the setup below runs automatically when you click **Run Code** here.)

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| setup: true
#| exercise: center_mean_median
library(palmerpenguins)
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
```

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: center_mean_median
mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
median(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="center_mean_median"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?mean` and `?median`: the first argument `x` is a numeric vector. By default `na.rm = FALSE`, so any `NA` makes the result `NA` — pass `na.rm = TRUE` to skip missing values.

Example with a built-in dataset:

```r
mean(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
median(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Apply the same pattern to the object named in the exercise prompt.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="center_mean_median"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
median(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Mean ≈ 4,202 g; median ≈ 4,050 g. The mean is pulled upward by a few heavy Gentoo penguins — that is why mean and median differ.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: center_mean_median
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("mean\\s*\\(", code) || !grepl("median\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Call both `mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)` and `median(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
} else if (!grepl("na\\.rm\\s*=\\s*TRUE", code, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Add `na.rm = TRUE` inside both `mean()` and `median()`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0(
      "Median ≈ ",
      round(.last_value, 0),
      " g. Compare it to the mean you printed — which is larger?"
    )
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Run both summaries on `body_mass` with `na.rm = TRUE`."
  )
}
```

## 3. Spread: standard deviation

`sd()` measures typical distance from the mean. Compute the standard deviation of `body_mass` with `na.rm = TRUE`.

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: spread_sd
sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="spread_sd"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?sd`: `sd(x, na.rm = FALSE)` measures spread around the mean in the **same units** as `x`. Like `mean()`, set `na.rm = TRUE` when the vector can contain missing values.

Example:

```r
sd(mtcars$hp, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Use `sd()` on the body-mass vector from this activity.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="spread_sd"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

You should see about 800 g. Standard deviation uses the **same units** as the data — grams, not grams squared.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: spread_sd
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("sd\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
} else if (!grepl("na\\.rm\\s*=\\s*TRUE", code, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Add `na.rm = TRUE` inside `sd()`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0("Spread ≈ ", round(.last_value, 0), " g — report sd in grams when you describe variation.")
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Run `sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
}
```

## 4. Variance vs. standard deviation

`var()` is sd squared, so its units are **grams²** — awkward for biology papers. Run `var()` and `sd()` on `body_mass` (both with `na.rm = TRUE`) and notice the difference in scale.

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: spread_var
var(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="spread_var"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?var`: variance has the same arguments as `sd()` — numeric vector `x`, and `na.rm` (default `FALSE`). Variance is in squared units; standard deviation is the square root and is easier to interpret in a sentence.

Compare both on the same column, for example:

```r
var(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Run both functions on the penguin body-mass vector here.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="spread_var"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
var(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Variance ≈ 640,000 g²; sd ≈ 800 g. For a sentence in a lab report, prefer sd in grams.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: spread_var
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("var\\s*\\(", code) || !grepl("sd\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Run both `var(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)` and `sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value) &&
             .last_value > 100 && .last_value < 2000) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = "Good — sd is in grams; variance is sd squared (grams²)."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Call `var()` and `sd()` on `body_mass` with `na.rm = TRUE`."
  )
}
```

## 5. Middle 50%: IQR

The **interquartile range** (`IQR()`) spans the middle half of the data — less sensitive to extreme values than sd. Compute it for `body_mass`.

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: spread_iqr
IQR(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="spread_iqr"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?IQR`: `IQR(x, na.rm = FALSE, type = 7)` returns the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles (middle 50% of the data). Use `na.rm = TRUE` when needed.

Example:

```r
IQR(mtcars$wt, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Call it on the vector named in the prompt.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="spread_iqr"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
IQR(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

IQR ≈ 1,200 g — the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: spread_iqr
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("IQR\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `IQR(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0("IQR ≈ ", round(.last_value, 0), " g — spread of the middle 50%.")
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Run `IQR(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
}
```

## 6. Five-number summary

`summary()` on a numeric vector prints min, quartiles, median, mean, and max in one call. Run it on `body_mass`.

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: summary_body_mass
summary(body_mass)
```

::: {.hint exercise="summary_body_mass"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?summary`: for a numeric vector, `summary()` prints min, quartiles, median, mean, and max in one table. No extra arguments are required for a simple numeric vector.

Example:

```r
summary(mtcars$disp)
```

Pass in the body-mass object you created earlier.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="summary_body_mass"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
summary(body_mass)
```

Use this as a quick sanity check before you write up results.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: summary_body_mass
#| check: true
```

## 7. Compare two species

Adelie and Gentoo penguins differ in size. The vectors below are ready — compute **mean** and **sd** for each (with `na.rm = TRUE`). No hypothesis test yet; just describe center and spread.

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| setup: true
#| exercise: compare_species
library(palmerpenguins)
adelie_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g[penguins$species == "Adelie"]
gentoo_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g[penguins$species == "Gentoo"]
```

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: compare_species
mean(adelie_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(adelie_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(gentoo_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(gentoo_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="compare_species"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

You already have two numeric vectors in memory. For **each** vector, call `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` and `sd(..., na.rm = TRUE)` — four lines total.

Practice the idea on `mtcars` by splitting on a category, then summarizing each subset:

```r
v4 <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl == 4]
v8 <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$cyl == 8]
mean(v4, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(v4, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Repeat for the second group, then do the same for the two species vectors in this exercise.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="compare_species"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean(adelie_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(adelie_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(gentoo_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(gentoo_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Gentoo mean body mass is higher; both groups show substantial spread around their means.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: global
#| exercise: compare_species
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
has_adelie <- grepl("adelie_mass", code) && grepl("mean\\s*\\(", code) && grepl("sd\\s*\\(", code)
has_gentoo <- grepl("gentoo_mass", code)
if (!has_adelie || !has_gentoo) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Compute `mean()` and `sd()` for both `adelie_mass` and `gentoo_mass`."
  )
} else if (grepl("na\\.rm\\s*=\\s*TRUE", code, ignore.case = TRUE) &&
             exists("adelie_mass", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE) &&
             exists("gentoo_mass", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  am <- mean(get("adelie_mass", envir = .envir_result), na.rm = TRUE)
  gm <- mean(get("gentoo_mass", envir = .envir_result), na.rm = TRUE)
  if (gm > am) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Gentoo center is higher; compare the sd values for spread within each species."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Re-run mean and sd for both `adelie_mass` and `gentoo_mass`."
    )
  }
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Run mean and sd on both species vectors with `na.rm = TRUE`."
  )
}
```

## 8. Recap

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Functions you used

| Function | What it tells you |
|----------|-------------------|
| `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Average (center) |
| `median(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Middle value (robust center) |
| `sd(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Typical deviation from the mean (spread, same units) |
| `var(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Squared spread (same units as data, squared) |
| `IQR(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Spread of the middle 50% |
| `summary()` | Min, quartiles, median, mean, max |

In **Coding Activity 5** you will visualize these distributions with ggplot2.
:::
